claim: Each Drosophila larval muscle is a single multinucleated fibre whose morphology reflects expression of distinctive identity Transcription Factors (iTFs).
source: Each Drosophila larval muscle is a single multinucleated fibre whose morphology reflects expression of distinctive identity Transcription Factors (iTFs).
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a foundational claim about Drosophila muscle structure and identity.

claim: Deletion of transcription cis-regulatory modules of Collier generates viable muscle identity mutants.
source: By deleting transcription cis-regulatory modules of one iTF, Collier, we generated viable muscle identity mutants, allowing live imaging and locomotion assays.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states that CRM deletions of Collier produced viable mutants used for experiments.

claim: Selection of muscle attachment sites is intrinsic to muscle identity.
source: We show that both selection of muscle attachment sites and muscle/muscle matching is intrinsic to muscle identity and requires transcriptional reprogramming of syncytial nuclei.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract.

claim: Muscle/muscle matching is intrinsic to muscle identity and requires transcriptional reprogramming of syncytial nuclei.
source: We show that both selection of muscle attachment sites and muscle/muscle matching is intrinsic to muscle identity and requires transcriptional reprogramming of syncytial nuclei.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract.

claim: The staggered muscle pattern involves attraction to tendon cells.
source: Live-imaging shows that the staggered muscle pattern involves attraction to tendon cells and heterotypic muscle-muscle adhesion.
evidence: This finding is based on live-imaging data presented in the study.

claim: The staggered muscle pattern involves heterotypic muscle-muscle adhesion.
source: Live-imaging shows that the staggered muscle pattern involves attraction to tendon cells and heterotypic muscle-muscle adhesion.
evidence: This finding is based on live-imaging data presented in the study.

claim: Unbalance in muscle identity leads to formation of branched muscles.
source: Unbalance leads to formation of branched muscles, and this correlates with locomotor behavior deficit.
evidence: This is stated as a finding in the abstract.

claim: Formation of branched muscles correlates with locomotor behavior deficit.
source: Unbalance leads to formation of branched muscles, and this correlates with locomotor behavior deficit.
evidence: This correlation is stated in the abstract as a finding from the study.

claim: The somatic musculature of the Drosophila larva consists of about 30 distinct body wall muscles per each hemi-segment distributed in three layers.
source: The somatic musculature of the Drosophila larva - about 30 distinct body wall muscles per each hemi-segment which are distributed in three layers, internal, median and external - is a model to study how a muscle pattern is specified and linked to locomotion behaviour.
evidence: This is a descriptive statement about Drosophila larval muscle anatomy.

claim: Each Drosophila larval muscle is a single multinucleated fibre with a specific identity including size, shape, orientation, motoneuron innervation and attachment sites.
source: Each muscle is a single multinucleated fibre with a specific identity: size, shape, orientation relative to the dorso-ventral and antero-posterior body axes, motoneuron innervation and attachment sites to the exoskeleton via tendon cells located at specific positions.
evidence: This describes the characteristics that define muscle identity in Drosophila larvae.

claim: Intersegmental tendon cells are distributed in three groups: dorsal, lateral and ventral.
source: Intersegmental tendon cells, where a large fraction of muscles is attached, are distributed in three groups, dorsal, lateral and ventral (Bate, 1990; Volk and VijayRaghavan, 1994; Schweitzer et al., 2010; Armand et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Internal muscles attach to muscle(s) in the next segment, forming 'indirect' muscle attachment sites (iMAS).
source: Internal muscles also attach to muscle(s) in the next segment, forming 'indirect' muscle attachment sites (iMAS) (Maartens and Brown, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Maartens and Brown, 2015.

claim: Drosophila muscle development proceeds through fusion of a founder myoblast (FC) with fusion-competent myoblasts (FCMs).
source: Drosophila muscle development proceeds through fusion of a founder myoblast (founder cell, FC) with fusion-competent myoblasts (FCMs) (Deng et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a well-established mechanism cited from Deng et al., 2017.

claim: Founder cells originate from asymmetric division of progenitor cells (PCs) selected from promuscular clusters (PMCs).
source: FCs originate from asymmetric division of progenitor cells (PCs) themselves selected from equivalence groups of myoblasts, called promuscular clusters (PMCs).
evidence: This describes the developmental origin of founder cells.

claim: Muscle identity ensues from the expression by each PC and FC of a specific combination of identity transcription factors (iTFs).
source: Muscle identity ensues from the expression by each PC and FC of a specific combination of identity transcription factors (iTFs) (de Joussineau et al., 2012), established in three steps
evidence: This is supported by citation to de Joussineau et al., 2012.

claim: iTF expression is established in three steps during muscle development.
source: Muscle identity ensues from the expression by each PC and FC of a specific combination of identity transcription factors (iTFs) (de Joussineau et al., 2012), established in three steps: First, different iTFs are activated in different PMCs, in response to positional information, and this expression is only maintained in PCs. Second, refinement of the iTF code occurs via cross-regulations between different iTFs in PCs and/or FCs and Notch signalling (Carmena et al., 1998; Carmena et al., 2002; Enriquez et al., 2010). Several PCs can be serially selected from a PMC and give rise to different muscle identities according to birth order, adding a temporal dimension to these regulations. A well-documented example is the distinction between DA2 and DA3 identities (Figure 1A; Dubois et al., 2016; Boukhatmi et al., 2012). Third, transcriptional activation of iTFs in syncytial nuclei after fusion correlates with the activation of identity 'realisation' genes acting downstream of some iTFs (Crozatier and Vincent, 1999; Knirr et al., 1999; Bataillé et al., 2010; Bataillé et al., 2017).
evidence: The three-step process is described with supporting citations.

claim: Different iTFs are activated in different PMCs in response to positional information, and this expression is only maintained in PCs.
source: First, different iTFs are activated in different PMCs, in response to positional information, and this expression is only maintained in PCs.
evidence: This describes the first step of iTF establishment.

claim: Refinement of the iTF code occurs via cross-regulations between different iTFs in PCs and/or FCs and Notch signalling.
source: Second, refinement of the iTF code occurs via cross-regulations between different iTFs in PCs and/or FCs and Notch signalling (Carmena et al., 1998; Carmena et al., 2002; Enriquez et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Several PCs can be serially selected from a PMC and give rise to different muscle identities according to birth order.
source: Several PCs can be serially selected from a PMC and give rise to different muscle identities according to birth order, adding a temporal dimension to these regulations.
evidence: This describes temporal regulation of muscle identity specification.

claim: The distinction between DA2 and DA3 identities is a well-documented example of birth order-dependent muscle identity specification.
source: A well-documented example is the distinction between DA2 and DA3 identities (Figure 1A; Dubois et al., 2016; Boukhatmi et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations and reference to Figure 1A.

claim: Transcriptional activation of iTFs in syncytial nuclei after fusion correlates with the activation of identity 'realisation' genes acting downstream of some iTFs.
source: Third, transcriptional activation of iTFs in syncytial nuclei after fusion correlates with the activation of identity 'realisation' genes acting downstream of some iTFs (Crozatier and Vincent, 1999; Knirr et al., 1999; Bataillé et al., 2010; Bataillé et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: col is transcribed in a dorso-lateral PMC from which several PCs are sequentially selected.
source: col transcription in myogenic lineages is first observed in a dorso-lateral PMC from which are sequentially selected several PCs (Dubois et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Dubois et al., 2016.

claim: col transcription is maintained in two PCs (DA3/DO5 and DT1/DO3), then one FC (DA3 FC), and is activated in FCM nuclei recruited into the DA3 growing fibre.
source: It is subsequently maintained in two PCs, then one FC, the DA3 FC, and is activated in FCM nuclei recruited into the DA3 growing fibre (Crozatier and Vincent, 1999; Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by citation and reference to Figure 1A.

claim: Two col CRMs (E-CRM and L-CRM) contain embryonic in vivo binding sites for Mef-2 and Twist.
source: Two col CRMs containing embryonic in vivo binding sites for the master myogenic TFs, Mef-2 and Twist (Twi) (Sandmann et al., 2007; Zinzen et al., 2009) were previously identified
evidence: This is supported by citations to Sandmann et al., 2007 and Zinzen et al., 2009.

claim: E-CRM is active in the PMC and the DA3/DO5 and DT1/DO3 PCs.
source: E-CRM, which is active in the PMC and the DA3/DO5 and DT1/DO3 PCs
evidence: This describes the activity pattern of E-CRM based on previous work.

claim: L-CRM is active in the DA3/DO5 and DT1/DO3 PCs, the DA3 FC and DA3 syncytial nuclei.
source: L-CRM which is active in these same 2 PCs, the DA3 FC and DA3 syncytial nuclei (Enriquez et al., 2010; Dubois et al., 2007; Figure 1A; Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This describes the activity pattern of L-CRM based on previous work and figures.

claim: GMR13B08 reproduces PMC Col expression and overlaps E-CRM.
source: A single reporter, GMR13B08, reproduces PMC Col expression and it overlaps E-CRM
evidence: This is based on systematic analysis of Gal4 reporter lines.

claim: GMR12G07 and GMR12H01 display DA3 expression and both partly overlap L-CRM.
source: two reporters, GMR12G07 and GMR12H01, display DA3 expression and they both partly overlap L-CRM (Figure 1B and data not shown)
evidence: This is based on systematic analysis of Gal4 reporter lines and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Only two col muscle CRMs exist based on systematic analysis of reporter lines covering 36 kb of the col genomic region.
source: We conducted a systematic analysis of Gal4 reporter lines (Manning et al., 2012; Kvon et al., 2014) covering 36 kb of the col genomic region. A single reporter, GMR13B08, reproduces PMC Col expression and it overlaps E-CRM, and two reporters, GMR12G07 and GMR12H01, display DA3 expression and they both partly overlap L-CRM (Figure 1B and data not shown), attesting to the existence of only two col muscle CRMs.
evidence: This conclusion is based on systematic reporter analysis.

claim: colΔL strains are homozygous viable and fertile.
source: colΔL strains are homozygous viable and fertile.
evidence: This is an observation about the viability of the mutant strains.

claim: colΔE strain is homozygous female sterile.
source: colΔE strain is homozygous female sterile, a sterility unrelated to col activity, since fertility is restored by placing colΔE over a deficiency (Df(2L)BSC429) (abbreviated Df in the rest of the text and figures) removing the entire col locus (data not shown).
evidence: This is an observation about the fertility of the mutant strain.

claim: The female sterility of colΔE is unrelated to col activity.
source: colΔE strain is homozygous female sterile, a sterility unrelated to col activity, since fertility is restored by placing colΔE over a deficiency (Df(2L)BSC429) (abbreviated Df in the rest of the text and figures) removing the entire col locus (data not shown).
evidence: This is inferred from the rescue experiment with the deficiency.

claim: In col1 homozygous mutant embryos, col transcription is detected at the PMC and PC stages and lost at the FC stage.
source: In col1 homozygous mutant embryos, col transcription is detected at the PMC and PC stages and lost at the FC stage, showing the key role of autoregulation in the maintenance of col transcription (Crozatier and Vincent, 1999; de Taffin et al., 2015).
evidence: This is based on in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Autoregulation plays a key role in the maintenance of col transcription.
source: In col1 homozygous mutant embryos, col transcription is detected at the PMC and PC stages and lost at the FC stage, showing the key role of autoregulation in the maintenance of col transcription (Crozatier and Vincent, 1999; de Taffin et al., 2015).
evidence: This is inferred from the col1 mutant phenotype and supported by citations.

claim: In colΔE embryos, col is not activated in PMC cells.
source: In colΔE embryos, we found that col is not activated in PMC cells, as could be expected.
evidence: This is based on in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: In colΔE embryos, col transcription is detected in the DA3/DO5 and DT1/DO3 PCs despite absence of PMC expression.
source: Yet, col transcription is detected in the DA3/DO5 and DT1/DO3 PCs, showing that inheritance of Col protein synthesised under E-CRM control is not required for activation of col transcription in PCs.
evidence: This is based on in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Inheritance of Col protein synthesised under E-CRM control is not required for activation of col transcription in PCs.
source: Yet, col transcription is detected in the DA3/DO5 and DT1/DO3 PCs, showing that inheritance of Col protein synthesised under E-CRM control is not required for activation of col transcription in PCs.
evidence: This is inferred from the colΔE phenotype.

claim: In colΔE embryos, a normal col expression pattern is observed in the developing DA3 muscle at stage 14.
source: A normal pattern is observed in the developing DA3 muscle, at stage 14.
evidence: This is based on in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: In colΔL1.3 embryos, col is transcribed in PMC cells and the DA3/DO5 and DT1/DO3 PCs, but not at stage 14.
source: Reciprocal to E-CRM deletion, col is transcribed in PMC cells and the DA3/DO5 and DT1/DO3 PCs in colΔL1.3 embryos, but no more at stage 14, showing that L-CRM is required for col transcription maintenance.
evidence: This is based on in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: L-CRM is required for col transcription maintenance.
source: Reciprocal to E-CRM deletion, col is transcribed in PMC cells and the DA3/DO5 and DT1/DO3 PCs in colΔL1.3 embryos, but no more at stage 14, showing that L-CRM is required for col transcription maintenance.
evidence: This is inferred from the colΔL1.3 phenotype.

claim: A PC-specific CRM exists within the −3.3 to −2.3 fragment of L-CRM, separate from the autoregulatory CRM.
source: Analysis of new col-lacZyi reporter genes (Perry et al., 2010) revealed the existence of a PC-specific CRM located within the −3.3 to −2.3 fragment of L-CRM, i.e., which is separate from the autoregulatory CRM defined by the in vivo Col binding site and contains the in vivo binding sites for Mef2 and Twist (Figure 1C; Figure 1—figure supplement 3; Zinzen et al., 2009).
evidence: This is based on reporter gene analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: The PC-specific CRM contains in vivo binding sites for Mef2 and Twist.
source: Analysis of new col-lacZyi reporter genes (Perry et al., 2010) revealed the existence of a PC-specific CRM located within the −3.3 to −2.3 fragment of L-CRM, i.e., which is separate from the autoregulatory CRM defined by the in vivo Col binding site and contains the in vivo binding sites for Mef2 and Twist (Figure 1C; Figure 1—figure supplement 3; Zinzen et al., 2009).
evidence: This is based on reporter gene analysis and cited binding site data.

claim: Activity of the PC-specific CRM is transient and lost upon removal of Mef2 and Twist binding sites.
source: Activity of this PC-specific CRM is transient and lost upon removal of Mef2 and Twist binding sites (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is based on reporter gene analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Two CRMs separately drive col transcription in muscle PCs.
source: Overall, we conclude that two CRMs separately drive col transcription in muscle PCs, suggesting that robust iTF expression at the PC stage is critical to confer a muscle its identity.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the CRM deletion and reporter analyses.

claim: Robust iTF expression at the PC stage is critical to confer a muscle its identity.
source: Overall, we conclude that two CRMs separately drive col transcription in muscle PCs, suggesting that robust iTF expression at the PC stage is critical to confer a muscle its identity.
evidence: This is inferred from the redundancy of CRMs at the PC stage.

claim: E-CRM and L-CRM act redundantly at the PC stage.
source: CRM deletions show that E-CRM and L-CRM act redundantly at the PC stage, emphasising that PC is a key stage in specification of muscle identity.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the CRM deletion analyses.

claim: PC is a key stage in specification of muscle identity.
source: CRM deletions show that E-CRM and L-CRM act redundantly at the PC stage, emphasising that PC is a key stage in specification of muscle identity.
evidence: This is inferred from the redundancy of CRMs at the PC stage.

claim: L-CRM deletion results in loss of col transcription in DA3 FCs and morphological transformation of the DA3 into a DA2-like muscle.
source: L-CRM deletion results into loss of col transcription in DA3 FCs and morphological transformation of the DA3 into a DA2-like muscle.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from the L-CRM deletion experiments.

claim: Removal of the col autoregulatory cis-module in L-CRM specifically abolishes col activation in syncytial nuclei fusing with the DA3 FC.
source: Removal of an auto-regulatory cis-module located in L-CRM specifically abolishes col activation in syncytial nuclei fusing with the DA3 FC.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from the colΔL0.5 deletion experiments.

claim: Removal of the col autoregulatory module leads to incomplete DA3 transformations and the formation of bifid/branched muscles of mixed DA3/DA2 morphology.
source: This leads to incomplete DA3 transformations and the formation of bifid/branched muscles of mixed DA3/DA2 morphology.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from the colΔL0.5 deletion experiments.

claim: The FC transcriptional program must be propagated to syncytial nuclei for a muscle to adopt a specific morphology.
source: In summary, our data show that i) the FC transcriptional program must be propagated to syncytial nuclei for a muscle to adopt a specific morphology
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the CRM deletion experiments.

claim: The precise matching of muscle/muscle attachments over the intersegmental border involves a process of selective adhesion controlled by iTFs.
source: ii) the precise matching of muscle/muscle attachments over the intersegmental border, which leads to a staggered rows pattern, involves a process of selective adhesion controlled by iTFs
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the live imaging and attachment site analyses.

claim: Branched muscles affect larval locomotion performance.
source: iii) branched muscles affect larval locomotion performance.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the locomotion assays.

claim: Branched muscles are typical of late, severe phases of human Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy.
source: Branched muscles are typical of late, severe phases of human Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy (Chan and Head, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Chan and Head, 2011.

claim: Drosophila iTF CRM deletion could be an effective setting for creating muscle-specific transformations and branched muscles as new paradigms to study myopathies.
source: Drosophila iTF CRM deletion could be an effective setting for creating muscle-specific transformations and branched muscles, as new paradigms to study myopathies specifically affecting subsets of muscles in humans.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion about the potential application of the approach.

claim: The DA3 morphology is normal in about 80% of segments in colΔE/Df embryos.
source: L-CRM-moeGFP expression at stage 15 shows that the DA3 morphology is normal in about 80% of segments in colΔE/Df embryos (Figure 2A–B)
evidence: This is based on quantification shown in Figure 2B.

claim: In colΔL1.3/Df embryos, the DA3 muscle is most often (85.2% of segments) transformed into a DA2-like muscle.
source: Low level GFP expression in colΔL1.3/Df embryos, consistent with col transcription data (Figure 1D), shows that the DA3 muscle is most often (85.2% of segments) transformed into a DA2-like muscle (designated below as DA3>DA2; Figure 2A–B), like in col null mutant embryos (Enriquez et al., 2012).
evidence: This is based on quantification shown in Figure 2B.

claim: In colΔL0.5/Df embryos, a high number (29%) of branched muscles is observed.
source: In colΔL0.5/Df embryos, i.e, when only the autoregulation module has been deleted, a high number (29%) of branched muscles is observed (Figure 2A–B).
evidence: This is based on quantification shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Branched muscles correspond to incomplete transformations, with two stable anterior attachment sites, overlapping the DA3 and DA2 sites in wt embryos.
source: Branched muscles correspond to incomplete transformations, with two stable anterior attachment sites, overlapping the DA3 and DA2 sites in wt embryos.
evidence: This is based on observation of the branched muscle phenotype.

claim: An iTF CRM deletion strategy is effective for creating viable muscle-specific identity mutants.
source: The high ratios of either complete (DA3>DA2) or incomplete (branched) transformations in L-CRM deletion mutants demonstrate that an iTF CRM deletion strategy is effective for creating viable muscle-specific identity mutants and explore branched muscle properties.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the success of the CRM deletion approach.

claim: Col is detected in PCs at stage 11 but not in muscles at stage 15 in either colΔL1.3 or colΔL0.5 deletion strains.
source: In either deletion strain, Col is detected in PCs at stage 11 but not in muscles at stage 15 (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is based on Col immunostaining shown in Figure 3A.

claim: At stage 14, some Col protein is still detected in muscle precursors in colΔL0.5, not in colΔL1.3 embryos.
source: However, at stage 14, some Col protein is still detected in muscle precursors in colΔL0.5, not in colΔL1.3 embryos (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is based on Col immunostaining shown in Figure 3B.

claim: In control wt/Df embryos, a col transcription dot is systematically detected in the DA3/DO5 PC (20/20 segments).
source: In control wt/Df embryos, a dot is systematically detected in the DA3/DO5 PC (20/20 segments; five embryos analysed)
evidence: This is based on FISH analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: In control wt/Df embryos, a col transcription dot is systematically detected in the DA3 FC (20/20 segments).
source: In control wt/Df embryos, a dot is systematically detected in the DA3/DO5 PC (20/20 segments; five embryos analysed), the DA3 FC (20/20)
evidence: This is based on FISH analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: In control wt/Df embryos, 80% of DA3 nuclei show col transcription at stage 14 (6 of 7–8 nuclei per fibre on average; 27 segments).
source: In control wt/Df embryos, a dot is systematically detected in the DA3/DO5 PC (20/20 segments; five embryos analysed), the DA3 FC (20/20) and 80% of DA3 nuclei at stage 14 (6 of 7–8 nuclei per fibre on average; 27 segments).
evidence: This is based on FISH analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: A col transcription dot is detected in the DA3/DO5 PC in colΔL1.3 (21/21) and colΔL0.5 (18/18) embryos, reflecting E-CRM activity.
source: A dot is detected as well in the DA3/DO5 PC, in either colΔL1.3 (21/21) or colΔL0.5 (18/18) embryos, reflecting E-CRM activity (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is based on FISH analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: In colΔL0.5 embryos, a col hybridisation dot is detected in the DA3 FC (19/19) and in one nucleus, likely the FC nucleus (11/21 segments), sometimes two nuclei at stage 14.
source: In colΔL0.5 embryos, a col hybridisation dot is detected in the DA3 FC (19/19) and in one nucleus, likely the FC nucleus (11/21 segments), sometimes two nuclei at stage 14.
evidence: This is based on FISH analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: In colΔL1.3 embryos, col transcription is only detected in a minor fraction of FCs (4/15) and is completely lost at stage 14 (0/6–7 nuclei per fibre on average; 24 segments).
source: In colΔL1.3 embryos, however, col transcription is only detected in a minor fraction of FCs (4/15) and is completely lost at stage 14 (0/6–7 nuclei per fibre on average; 24 segments).
evidence: This is based on FISH analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Similar levels of col transcription are found in the DA3 PC in control (Mean ± sem: 1.22 ± 0.06; n = 18), colΔL1.3 (1.15 ± 0.04; n = 26) and colΔL0.5 embryos (1.19 ± 0.04; n = 18).
source: As expected, similar levels of col transcription are found in the DA3 PC, in control (Mean ± sem: 1.22 ± 0.06; n = 18), colΔL1.3 (1.15 ± 0.04; n = 26) and colΔL0.5 embryos (1.19 ± 0.04; n = 18), which confirms handling by the E-CRM, with only a minor contribution from the L-CRM (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is based on quantification of col transcripts shown in Figure 3D.

claim: High level of col transcription in the DA3 FC in wt embryos (2.20 ± 0.05; n = 28) is dependent upon L-CRM activity.
source: On the contrary, high level of col transcription in the DA3 FC in wt embryos (2.20 ± 0.05; n = 28) is dependent upon L-CRM activity, since a drop is observed in colΔL1.3 FCs (1.10 ± 0.04; n = 24), p<0.001.
evidence: This is based on quantification of col transcripts shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The high level of col transcription in the DA3 FC is dependent upon the presence of Mef2 and Twist binding sites.
source: More precisely, it is dependent upon the presence of Mef2 and Twist binding sites since a basal level of transcription is still observed when only the col autoregulation module is deleted (colΔL0.5: 1.41 ± 0.04; n = 25).
evidence: This is based on quantification of col transcripts shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The col/nau increase between the PC and FC stages in wt embryo is due to increased col transcription while the level of nau is relatively constant.
source: Quantification of col and nau transcripts shows that the col/nau increase between the PC and FC stages in wt embryo is due to increased col transcription while the level of nau is relatively constant and is unaffected in col L-CRM mutants (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on quantification shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Binding of Mef2 and Twist is required to prime col transcription in the FC nucleus before autoregulation takes off.
source: Together, the data suggest that binding of Mef2 and Twist is required to prime col transcription in the FC nucleus before autoregulation takes off (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is inferred from the transcription quantification data.

claim: Sustained col transcription in the FC nucleus in colΔL0.5 embryos provides enough Col protein for some uptake by other DA3 nuclei at stage 14.
source: Taken with one another, Col immunostaining, FISH data and col transcription quantification indicate that sustained col transcription in the FC nucleus in colΔL0.5 embryos (Figure 3C–D), provides enough Col protein for some uptake by other DA3 nuclei at stage 14, and this leads to their partial reprogramming to DA3 identity.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined data.

claim: Partial reprogramming of syncytial nuclei could explain the formation of branched muscles retaining some DA3 morphological characters.
source: Partial reprogramming could, in turn, explain the formation of branched muscles retaining some DA3 morphological characters.
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between partial reprogramming and branched muscle phenotype.

claim: Both iTF transcription in the FC and reprogramming of 'naïve' syncytial nuclei contribute to ensure robust muscle morphological identity.
source: Moreover, the colΔL1.3 and colΔL0.5 expression data and deletion phenotypes show that both iTF transcription in the FC and reprogramming of 'naïve' syncytial nuclei contribute to ensure robust muscle morphological identity (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the combined data from both deletion strains.

claim: In wt embryos, the DA3 posterior edge anchors to dorsal, and anterior edge to lateral intersegmental tendon cells.
source: Double staining of ready-to-hatch (st17) wt embryos for F-actin and Ilk-GFP, a component of muscle attachment sites (Zervas et al., 2011; Sarov et al., 2016) shows that the DA3 posterior edge anchors to dorsal, and anterior edge to lateral intersegmental tendon cells (Figure 4A), giving its final acute shape (Bate, 1990).
evidence: This is based on immunostaining shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The DA3 and DA2, as well as the DA2 and DA1 muscles precisely align with each other over each intersegmental border, forming heterotypic muscle-muscle attachment (iMAS).
source: Moreover, the DA3 and DA2, as well as the DA2 and DA1 muscles precisely align with each other over each intersegmental border, forming heterotypic muscle-muscle attachment (iMAS; [Maartens and Brown, 2015]) at the origin of the staggered rows disposition of DA muscles.
evidence: This is based on immunostaining shown in Figure 4A.

claim: No DA3/DA3 (homotypic) iMAS surface is observed in wt embryos.
source: No DA3/DA3 (homotypic) iMAS surface is observed (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is based on immunostaining shown in Figure 4A.

claim: In colΔL1.3 embryos, the anterior edge of DA3>DA2 transformed muscles anchors to dorsal tendon cells instead of lateral intersegmental tendon cells.
source: On the contrary, in colΔL1.3 embryos, the anterior edge of DA3>DA2 transformed muscles anchors to dorsal tendon cells instead of lateral intersegmental tendon cells, leading to a 'dual DA3>DA2 morphology', DA2-like at the anterior, and DA3 at the posterior edge.
evidence: This is based on immunostaining shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The dual identity of DA3>DA2 muscles leads to iMASs between adjacent DA3>DA2 muscles.
source: This dual identity leads to iMASs between adjacent DA3>DA2 muscles (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is based on immunostaining shown in Figure 4A.

claim: In colΔL1.3 embryos, DA2 iMASs are shifted dorsally and the general pattern of DA muscles is affected.
source: As a consequence, DA2 iMASs are shifted dorsally and the general pattern of DA muscles is affected.
evidence: This is based on immunostaining shown in Figure 4A.

claim: In wt embryos between stages 12 and 13, the DA3 muscle precursor extends protrusions towards dorsal tendon cells posteriorly, and both dorsal and lateral tendon cells anteriorly.
source: In wt embryos between stages 12 and 13 (Video 1; Figure 4B), the DA3 muscle precursor extends protrusions towards dorsal tendon cells, posteriorly, and both dorsal and lateral tendon cells, anteriorly, diverging from a bipolar extension scheme (Schnorrer and Dickson, 2004).
evidence: This is based on live imaging shown in Video 1 and Figure 4B.

claim: At stage 14 in wt embryos, the posterior DA3 edge makes contacts with dorsal tendon cells before the anterior edge(s) reaches the intersegmental border.
source: At stage 14, the posterior DA3 edge makes contacts with dorsal tendon cells before the anterior edge(s) reaches the intersegmental border, a time gap previously observed during live-imaging of a ventro-lateral muscle (Gilsohn and Volk, 2010).
evidence: This is based on live imaging shown in Video 1 and Figure 4B.

claim: Numerous filopodia emanate from the DA3 dorsal surface and contact the DA2 ventral surface at stage 14 in wt embryos.
source: In addition, numerous filopodia emanate from the DA3 dorsal surface and contact the DA2 ventral surface, contributing to give the DA3 muscle precursor its transient angled-shape.
evidence: This is based on live imaging shown in Video 1 and Figure 4B.

claim: At late stage 14 in wt embryos, the posterior DA3 attachment widens parallel to the intersegmental border.
source: At late stage 14, the posterior DA3 attachment widens parallel to the intersegmental border.
evidence: This is based on live imaging shown in Video 1 and Figure 4B.

claim: At late stage 14 in wt embryos, the anterior DA3 attachment to lateral tendon cells becomes stable, whereas dorsal anterior filipodia appear to be repelled from the intersegmental border.
source: Its anterior attachment to lateral tendon cells in turn becomes stable, whereas dorsal anterior filipodia appear to be repelled from the intersegmental border where the DA3 muscle in the preceding segment is attached.
evidence: This is based on live imaging shown in Video 1 and Figure 4B.

claim: In colΔL1.3 embryos, the main axis of the DA3>DA2 muscle precursor elongation is more longitudinal than wt, already at stage 12.
source: In colΔL1.3 embryos, the main axis of the DA3>DA2 muscle precursor elongation is more longitudinal than wt, already at stage 12 (Video 2; Figure 4B).
evidence: This is based on live imaging shown in Video 2 and Figure 4B.

claim: In colΔL1.3 embryos, protrusions contacting dorsal tendon cells do not retract at later stages when they contact the DA3>DA2 muscle from the preceding segment.
source: At stage 13 and like in wt, many protrusions emanate from the DA3 dorsal surface, but unlike in wt, protrusions contacting dorsal tendon cells do not retract at later stages when they contact the DA3>DA2 muscle from the preceding segment.
evidence: This is based on live imaging shown in Video 2 and Figure 4B.

claim: Stabilisation of contacts made by protrusions in colΔL1.3 embryos prefigures abnormal DA3>DA2/DA3>DA2 iMAS formation.
source: Rather, stabilisation of contacts made by these protrusions prefigures abnormal DA3>DA2/DA3>DA2 iMAS formation (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is inferred from the live imaging observations.

claim: In some segments of colΔL1.3 embryos, contacts with lateral tendon cells are also stabilised, resulting into branched muscles.
source: In some segments, contacts with lateral tendon cells are also stabilised, resulting into branched muscles.
evidence: This is based on live imaging shown in Video 2 and Figure 4B.

claim: The posterior edge of DA3 precisely aligns with the anterior edge of DA2 in control embryos at stage 16.
source: Expressing together VgM1-mCD8GFP-H2bRFP, L-CRM-moeGFP and stripeGal4:UAS-mCD8RFP, and co-staining of stage 16 control embryos for α-Spectrin, a protein enriched at muscle attachment sites, shows that the posterior edge of DA3 precisely aligns with the anterior edge of DA2 (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1), suggesting heterotypic attractive cues.
evidence: This is based on immunostaining shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Heterotypic DA3/DA2 attraction is already observed at stage 14, when the dorsal DA3 and ventral DA2 surfaces contact each other via numerous protrusions.
source: This attraction is already observed at stage 14, when the dorsal DA3 and ventral DA2 surfaces contact each other via numerous protrusions (Figure 5A and B; Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on immunostaining shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: At stage 15 in wt embryos, the DA3/DA2 contact zone gets away from intersegmental borders and the DA3/DA3 and DA2/DA2 homotypic connections disappear, to give way to heterotypic DA3/DA2 stable iMAS formation.
source: Strikingly, at stage 15, the contact zone gets away from intersegmental borders and the DA3/DA3 and DA2/DA2 homotypic connections disappear, to give way to heterotypic DA3/DA2 stable iMAS formation.
evidence: This is based on immunostaining shown in Figure 5A.

claim: In colΔL1.3 embryos, the initial steps at stages 14 and 15 are similar to wt, except for the absence of stable connection of DA3>DA2 to lateral tendon cells.
source: In colΔL1.3 embryos, the initial steps, stages 14 and 15, are similar to wt, except for the absence of stable connection of DA3>DA2 to lateral tendon cells, as seen by live imaging (Video 2).
evidence: This is based on immunostaining shown in Figure 5A and live imaging in Video 2.

claim: At stage 16 in colΔL1.3 embryos, DA3>DA2/DA3>DA2 and DA3>DA2/DA2 iMASs are privileged, while no homotypic DA2/DA2 iMAS forms.
source: At stage 16, DA3>DA2/DA3>DA2 and DA3>DA2/DA2 iMASs are privileged, while similar to control, no homotypic DA2/DA2 iMAS forms, suggesting homotypic repulsion (Figure 4; Figure 5A).
evidence: This is based on immunostaining shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The precise pattern of iMASs and muscles is contributed by a combination of attractive and, possibly, repulsive cues downstream of muscle iTFs.
source: Together, the data indicate that the precise pattern of iMASs and muscles is contributed by a combination of attractive and, possibly, repulsive cues downstream of muscle iTFs (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the combined data from imaging and mutant analyses.

claim: The fraction of DA3, DA3>DA2 and branched muscles in 3rd instar larvae conforms to the statistics in late embryos, except for an increased proportion of branched muscles.
source: It conforms to the statistics in late embryos (Figure 2B), except for an increased proportion of branched muscles, which could reflect under-evaluation of their number in embryos, due to threshold detection limit of L-CRM-moeGFP expression in thin fibres (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is based on quantification shown in Figure 6B.

claim: In wt larvae, the anterior edge of the DA3 muscle is anchored to a nodal lateral attachment site shared with the LL1 muscle.
source: In wt larvae, as seen in stage 17 embryos (Figure 4A), the anterior edge of the DA3 muscle is anchored to a nodal lateral attachment site shared with the LL1 muscle
evidence: This is based on SEM analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claim: In wt larvae, the posterior edge of DA3 aligns with the anterior edge of the DA2 muscle in the next posterior segment.
source: while its posterior edge aligns with the anterior edge of the DA2 muscle in the next posterior segment.
evidence: This is based on SEM analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The regular alignment of the DA1, DA2 and DA3 muscles draws strength lines spanning three adjacent segments in wt larvae.
source: The regular alignment of the DA1, DA2 and DA3 muscles both draws strength lines spanning three adjacent segments, and regular tension surfaces between segments (Figure 6C; Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on SEM analysis shown in Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: In colΔL1.3 larvae, the anterior DA3 muscle attachment has shifted from lateral to dorsal to form a DA3>DA2/DA3>DA2 homotypic iMAS.
source: In colΔL1.3 larvae, the anterior DA3 muscle attachment has shifted from lateral to dorsal to form a DA3>DA2/DA3>DA2 homotypic iMAS (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is based on SEM analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The shift in DA3 attachment in colΔL1.3 larvae leads to the formation of narrow, ectopic DA2/DA2 contacts and distortion of the DA1-DA2-DA3 strength line.
source: This leads in turn to the formation of narrow, ectopic DA2/DA2 contacts and the DA1-DA2-DA3 strength line is distorted (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on SEM analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: In case of branched DA3 muscles, two strength lines co-exist.
source: In case of branched DA3 muscles, two strength lines co-exist (Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on SEM analysis shown in Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Loss of DA3 identity leads to ectopic iMASs between several dorsal internal muscles, distortion of the staggered ends architecture of DA muscles and of their alignment between consecutive segments.
source: In conclusion, SEM analyses of larval muscles show that loss of DA3 identity leads to ectopic iMASs between several dorsal internal muscles, distortion of the staggered ends architecture of DA muscles and of their alignment between consecutive segments.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on SEM analyses.

claim: colΔL0.5/Df larvae display a significantly reduced crawling speed (1.05 ± 0.034 mm/sec, n = 108) compared to +/Df controls (1.15 ± 0.031 mm/sec, n = 118), (p=0.03).
source: Beyond this variability, we observe, however, that colΔL0.5/Df larvae display a significantly reduced crawling speed on average 1.05 ± 0.034 mm/sec (n = 108), compared to 1.15 ± 0.031 mm/sec for +/Df controls (n = 118), (p=0.03) (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is based on locomotion assays shown in Figure 7A.

claim: A significantly shorter stride was measured for colΔL0.5/Df larvae (1.08 ± 0.025 mm) compared to control +/Df larvae (1.17 ± 0.024 mm), (p=0.008).
source: A significantly shorter stride was measured for colΔL0.5/Df larvae (1.08 ± 0.025 mm) compared to control +/Df larvae (1.17 ± 0.024 mm), (p=0.008).
evidence: This is based on locomotion assays shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Stride duration was extended from (1.09 ± 0.014 s) for +/Df larvae to 1.15 ± 0.017 s for colΔL0.5/Df larvae.
source: Furthermore, stride duration was extended, from (1.09 ± 0.014 s) for +/Df larvae to 1.15 ± 0.017 s for colΔL0.5/Df larvae.
evidence: This is based on locomotion assays shown in Figure 7C.

claim: colΔL1.3/Df larvae (n = 112) display intermediate values for crawling speed, stride length and stride duration, with differences falling below the significance threshold level.
source: For both crawling speed, stride length and stride duration, colΔL1.3/Df larvae (n = 112) display intermediate values. Yet, differences with either control or colΔL1.3/Df larvae fall below the significance threshold level, suggesting that mis-orientation of the DA3>DA2 muscle does not, by itself, significantly impair the efficiency of segment contraction.
evidence: This is based on locomotion assays shown in Figure 7.

claim: Mis-orientation of the DA3>DA2 muscle does not, by itself, significantly impair the efficiency of segment contraction.
source: Yet, differences with either control or colΔL1.3/Df larvae fall below the significance threshold level, suggesting that mis-orientation of the DA3>DA2 muscle does not, by itself, significantly impair the efficiency of segment contraction.
evidence: This is inferred from the locomotion assay results.

claim: In wt embryos, the MN projection which innervates DA3 leaves the ISN ventral to the DA3 position and orients left such that the neuromuscular junction locates to the first anterior third of the muscle (100%; n = 28 segments).
source: In wt embryos, the MN projection which innervates DA3 leaves the ISN ventral to the DA3 position and orients left such that the neuromuscular junction locates to the first anterior third of the muscle (100%; n = 28 segments).
evidence: This is based on anti-HRP and phalloidin staining shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: In case of a complete DA3>DA2 transformation, a MN projection is still observed (100%; n = 15 segments), which leaves the ISN at a more dorsal position than wt.
source: In case of a complete DA3>DA2 transformation, a MN projection is still observed (100%; n = 15 segments), which leaves the ISN at a more dorsal position than wt, reflecting the dorsal shift of the DA3>DA2, relative to DA3 muscle.
evidence: This is based on anti-HRP and phalloidin staining shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: In case of branched muscles, the lower branch is always innervated (100%, n = 30 segments).
source: In case of branched muscles, the lower branch is always innervated (100%, n = 30 segments).
evidence: This is based on anti-HRP and phalloidin staining shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Only in 20% of the cases, the second, upper branch of branched muscles is also innervated.
source: Only in 20% of the cases, the second, upper branch is also innervated.
evidence: This is based on anti-HRP and phalloidin staining shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Fully transformed DA3 muscles are innervated.
source: These innervation data indicate that fully transformed DA3 muscles are innervated, but only one branch of branched muscles is, in most cases.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the innervation data.

claim: Only one branch of branched muscles is innervated in most cases.
source: These innervation data indicate that fully transformed DA3 muscles are innervated, but only one branch of branched muscles is, in most cases.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the innervation data.

claim: Asymmetric innervation of branched muscles may contribute to the reduced crawling speed of colΔL0.5 larvae.
source: It remains to be established whether this asymmetric innervation contributes to the reduced crawling speed of colΔL0.5 larvae.
evidence: This is stated as an open question based on the innervation observations.

claim: Reporter analyses indicated that col transcription is controlled by two sequentially acting CRMs, of overlapping activity at the PC step.
source: Reporter analyses indicated that col transcription is controlled by two sequentially acting CRMs, of overlapping activity at the PC step, suggesting a handover mechanism between CRMs at this stage (Enriquez et al., 2012).
evidence: This is based on previous reporter analyses cited from Enriquez et al., 2012.

claim: L-CRM activity in PCs is not dependent, but redundant with E-CRM activity.
source: However, deletion analyses show that L-CRM activity in PCs is not dependent, but redundant with E-CRM activity, and can be separated from col positive autoregulation that is specific to the DA3 lineage.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the CRM deletion analyses.

claim: iTF code refinement at each step of muscle identity specification (PMC >PC, PC >FC and FC >syncytial nuclei) is driven by a separate CRM.
source: This leads to a new model where iTF code refinement at each step of muscle identity specification, PMC >PC, PC >FC and FC >syncytial nuclei, is driven by a separate CRM.
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the CRM deletion analyses.

claim: Distribution of the PC-identity information into two CRMs supports the idea that iTF regulation at the PC stage is nodal to muscle identity specification.
source: Distribution of the PC-identity information into two CRMs further supports the idea that iTF regulation at the PC stage is nodal to muscle identity specification (Carmena et al., 1998; Dubois et al., 2016; Enriquez et al., 2012; Jagla et al., 2002; Nose et al., 1998; Kumar et al., 2015).
evidence: This is inferred from the redundancy of CRMs and supported by citations.

claim: Combinatorial control of each dorso-lateral muscle identity involves at least eight different iTFs, in addition to Nau/MRF.
source: Our former analysis started to decrypt the combinatorial control of each dorso-lateral muscle identity, which involves at least eight different iTFs, in addition to Nau/MRF [Dubois et al., 2007].
evidence: This is based on previous analysis cited from Dubois et al., 2007.

claim: Persistent, low level expression of Col protein in the DT1 and LL1 muscle precursors upon removal of the col autoregulatory module suggests the existence of both positively and negatively acting iTF-responsive elements in this module.
source: Persistent, low level expression of Col protein in the DT1 and LL1 muscle precursors upon removal of the col autoregulatory module suggests the existence of both positively and negatively acting iTF-responsive elements in this module.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of persistent Col expression.

claim: Morphological transformations of other dorso-lateral muscles are observed at variable frequency in col protein null mutants.
source: Morphological transformations of other dorso-lateral muscles are observed at variable frequency in col protein null mutants (Enriquez et al., 2010)
evidence: This is based on previous observations cited from Enriquez et al., 2010.

claim: E-CRM activity provides robustness to the combinatorial control of identity of dorso-lateral muscles.
source: suggesting that E-CRM activity provides robustness to the combinatorial control of identity of these muscles and that robustness is likely also contributed by other iTFs (Dubois et al., 2016; Schnorrer and Dickson, 2004).
evidence: This is inferred from the variable frequency of transformations in col null mutants.

claim: PC/FC specific CRMs have only been functionally identified for a handful of muscle iTFs.
source: PC/FC specific CRMs have only been functionally identified for a handful of muscle iTFs (Rivera et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Rivera et al., 2019.

claim: Computational predictions identified several thousand putative muscle enhancers.
source: Computational predictions identified, however, several thousand putative muscle enhancers and uncovered extensive heterogeneity among the combinations of transcription factor binding sites in validated enhancers, beside sites for the core intrinsic muscle regulators Tin, Mef2 and Twi (Sandmann et al., 2007; Gisselbrecht et al., 2013; Cusanovich et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to computational studies.

claim: Fusing FCM nuclei generally adopt the iTF protein code of the FC nucleus.
source: Fusing FCM nuclei generally adopt the iTF protein code of the FC nucleus, while propagation of iTF transcription and activation of realisation genes is muscle lineage-specific (Boukhatmi et al., 2012; Crozatier and Vincent, 1999; Knirr et al., 1999; Bataillé et al., 2010; Bataillé et al., 2017; Bourgouin et al., 1992).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Propagation of iTF transcription and activation of realisation genes is muscle lineage-specific.
source: Fusing FCM nuclei generally adopt the iTF protein code of the FC nucleus, while propagation of iTF transcription and activation of realisation genes is muscle lineage-specific (Boukhatmi et al., 2012; Crozatier and Vincent, 1999; Knirr et al., 1999; Bataillé et al., 2010; Bataillé et al., 2017; Bourgouin et al., 1992).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Col protein import precedes activation of col transcription in fused FCM nuclei.
source: We have previously shown that Col protein import precedes activation of col transcription in fused FCM nuclei, and correlates with the activation of realisation genes, a sequence of events termed syncytial identity reprogramming (Bataillé et al., 2017; Dubois et al., 2007).
evidence: This is based on previous work cited from Bataillé et al., 2017 and Dubois et al., 2007.

claim: Final selection of myotendinous connection sites is intrinsic to FC identity.
source: From this, two conclusions can be drawn: 1) Final selection of myotendinous connection sites is intrinsic to FC identity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the CRM deletion experiments.

claim: Identity reprogramming of syncytial nuclei is required for robustness of myotendinous connection site selection and precise muscle patterns.
source: 2) Identity reprogramming of syncytial nuclei is required for robustness of this selection and precise muscle patterns.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the CRM deletion experiments.

claim: Live imaging of lateral-oblique and ventral transverse muscles development distinguished 3 phases of muscle elongation: FC migration (stage 12), bipolar myotube elongation (stages 13 to 15), and maturation of myotendinous attachment (stage 16).
source: Live imaging of lateral-oblique and ventral transverse muscles development distinguished 3 phases of muscle elongation (Schnorrer and Dickson, 2004): 1) FC migration, stage 12, ending with the first FC/FCM fusion event and stretching of the muscle precursor along a given axis; 2) bipolar myotube elongation, characterised by the presence of extensive filopodia at both axis ends, in search for attachment sites, stages 13 to 15; 3) maturation of myotendinous attachment, stage 16.
evidence: This is based on previous live imaging work cited from Schnorrer and Dickson, 2004.

claim: The formation of DA3>DA2 and branched muscles in CRM mutants recalls a transient exploration by the wt DA3 muscle precursor of both dorsal and lateral tendon cells.
source: The formation of DA3>DA2 and branched muscles in CRM mutants recalls a transient exploration by the wt DA3 muscle precursor of both dorsal and lateral tendon cells, a process deviating from the bipolar migration/attachment scheme (Schweitzer et al., 2010; Enriquez et al., 2012; Schnorrer and Dickson, 2004; Bahri et al., 2009).
evidence: This is inferred from comparison of mutant and wild-type phenotypes.

claim: Ectopic Col expression in the DA2 muscle leads to reciprocal DA2>DA3 transformation as well as branched muscles.
source: Interestingly, ectopic Col expression in the DA2 muscle leads to reciprocal DA2>DA3 transformation as well as branched muscles (Boukhatmi et al., 2012).
evidence: This is based on previous work cited from Boukhatmi et al., 2012.

claim: Selection of dorsal versus lateral tendon cells is a highly controlled process.
source: This indicates that selection of dorsal versus lateral tendon cells is a highly controlled process.
evidence: This is inferred from the reciprocal transformation experiments.

claim: Kon tiki/Perdido and DGrip are involved in proper elongation of ventral longitudinal muscles.
source: A few molecules involved in targeted attachment of subsets of muscles to specific tendon cells have been identified: Kon tiki/Perdido, a single pass transmembrane protein and the PDZ protein DGrip for proper elongation of ventral longitudinal muscles (Schnorrer et al., 2007)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Schnorrer et al., 2007.

claim: The ArfGAp protein Git is involved in sensing integrin signaling and halting elongation of Lateral Transverse (LT) muscles once their attachment site has been reached.
source: the ArfGAp protein Git for sensing integrin signaling and halting elongation of Lateral Transverse (LT) muscles once their attachment site has been reached (Bahri et al., 2009; Richier et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bahri et al., 2009 and Richier et al., 2018.

claim: Robo/Slit signaling attracts muscles at segmental borders.
source: Robo/Slit signaling attracts muscles at segmental borders, the Slit ligand being expressed by tendons, and Robo and Robo2 receptors by elongating muscles.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of Robo/Slit signaling.

claim: slit acts as a short-range repellent contributing to the collapse of leading-edge filopodia when a muscle reaches the tendon extracellular matrix.
source: slit also acts as a short-range repellent contributing to the collapse of leading-edge filopodia when a muscle reaches the tendon extracellular matrix (Ordan and Volk, 2015; Ordan et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ordan and Volk, 2015 and Ordan et al., 2015.

claim: In vivo imaging showed that the DA3 muscle fails to stop at the segment border in slit mutants and sometimes branches.
source: In vivo imaging showed that the DA3 muscle fails to stop at the segment border in slit mutants and sometimes branches (Ordan et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ordan et al., 2015.

claim: The DA3 slit branching pattern is similar to that frequently observed in nau mutants, with two posterior attachment sites in place of one.
source: However, this is not observed in colΔLCRM; the DA3 slit branching pattern is rather similar to that frequently observed in nau mutants, with two posterior attachment sites in place of one (Dubois et al., 2016; Boukhatmi et al., 2012).
evidence: This is based on comparison with nau mutants cited from Dubois et al., 2016 and Boukhatmi et al., 2012.

claim: Internal muscles attach to each other.
source: In addition to attaching to tendon cells, it was previously shown that internal muscles attach to each other (Maartens and Brown, 2015; Bate and Rushton, 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Maartens and Brown, 2015 and Bate and Rushton, 1993.

claim: DA3/DA2 matching in wt embryos results from both heterotypic DA3/DA2 attraction and, possibly, homotypic repulsion.
source: Recording DA3 and DA3>DA2 muscle development by a combination of live imaging and immunostainings shows that DA3/DA2 matching in wt embryos results from both heterotypic DA3/DA2 attraction and, possibly, homotypic repulsion.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on live imaging and immunostaining data.

claim: Prior attachment of the posterior DA3 edge to dorsal tendon cells leads to retraction of filopodia issued from the homologous muscle in the next adjacent segment.
source: Prior attachment of the posterior DA3 edge to dorsal tendon cells leads to retraction of filopodia issued from the homologous muscle in the next adjacent segment while stabilisation of heterotypic contacts results into DA3/DA2 iMAS formation over the intersegmental border.
evidence: This is based on live imaging observations.

claim: Stabilisation of heterotypic contacts results into DA3/DA2 iMAS formation over the intersegmental border.
source: Prior attachment of the posterior DA3 edge to dorsal tendon cells leads to retraction of filopodia issued from the homologous muscle in the next adjacent segment while stabilisation of heterotypic contacts results into DA3/DA2 iMAS formation over the intersegmental border.
evidence: This is based on live imaging observations.

claim: DA3>DA2 establish both homotypic iMASs, and heterotypic iMASs with DA2, suggesting preserved attraction to tendon cells and partial loss of preferential heterotypic adhesion.
source: Interestingly, DA3>DA2 establish both homotypic iMASs, and heterotypic iMASs with DA2, suggesting preserved attraction to tendon cells and partial loss of preferential heterotypic adhesion.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of both types of iMASs in DA3>DA2 muscles.

claim: Prior posterior attachment was previously observed during development of abdominal adult muscles.
source: Prior posterior attachment was previously observed during development of abdominal adult muscles (Currie and Bate, 1991).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Currie and Bate, 1991.

claim: Selective filopodia adhesion ensures precise matching between identical cardioblasts and boundaries between different cell identities in the Drosophila heart.
source: Cell matching is a widely used process during embryogenesis to construct complex tissue architecture. Selective filopodia adhesion has recently been shown to ensure precise matching between identical cardioblasts and boundaries between different cell identities in the Drosophila heart.
evidence: This is based on recent findings in heart development.

claim: Homotypic matching in the Drosophila heart is linked to differential expression by each cell type of the adhesion molecules, Fasciclin III and Ten-m.
source: In this case, homotypic matching is linked to differential expression by each cell type of the adhesion molecules, Fasciclin III and Ten-m (Zhang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2018.

claim: Drosophila larval crawling is a well-suited paradigm to link muscle contraction patterns and locomotor behaviour.
source: Drosophila larval crawling is a well-suited paradigm to link muscle contraction patterns and locomotor behaviour.
evidence: This is a statement about the utility of the Drosophila larval crawling model.

claim: Longitudinal, acute and oblique muscles within a larval segment contract together and, as they begin to relax, the contraction is propagated to the next segment, creating a peristaltic wave.
source: Longitudinal, acute and oblique muscles within a larval segment contract together and, as they begin to relax, the contraction is propagated to the next segment, creating a peristaltic wave from tail to head (forward locomotion), or head to tail (backward locomotion) (Heckscher et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Heckscher et al., 2012.

claim: The crawling speed during the escape response is not significantly reduced in colΔL1.3/Df, compared to control +/Df larvae.
source: The crawling speed during the escape response is not significantly reduced in colΔL1.3/Df, compared to control +/Df larvae, indicating that muscle contraction is properly controlled and that a mechanical compensation mechanism for the DA3 mis-orientation could occur.
evidence: This is based on locomotion assay results.

claim: Muscle contraction is properly controlled in colΔL1.3/Df larvae.
source: The crawling speed during the escape response is not significantly reduced in colΔL1.3/Df, compared to control +/Df larvae, indicating that muscle contraction is properly controlled and that a mechanical compensation mechanism for the DA3 mis-orientation could occur.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of significant crawling speed reduction.

claim: A mechanical compensation mechanism for the DA3 mis-orientation could occur in colΔL1.3/Df larvae.
source: The crawling speed during the escape response is not significantly reduced in colΔL1.3/Df, compared to control +/Df larvae, indicating that muscle contraction is properly controlled and that a mechanical compensation mechanism for the DA3 mis-orientation could occur.
evidence: This is speculated based on the lack of significant crawling speed reduction.

claim: Single muscle transformations only moderately impact crawling speed, raising the possibility of biomechanical compensation by other muscles.
source: From these different observations, we can conclude: i) single muscle transformations only moderately impact crawling speed, raising the possibility of biomechanical compensation by other muscles
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the locomotion assay results.

claim: Branched muscles could be less efficient than fully transformed muscles.
source: ii) branched muscles could be less efficient than fully transformed muscles.
evidence: This is inferred from the locomotion assay results.

claim: Branched muscle fibres accumulate in humans following muscle regeneration after damage or in Duchenne muscular dystrophy patients.
source: The generation of branched muscles in Drosophila identity mutants is one important finding as branched muscle fibres accumulate in humans, following muscle regeneration after damage or in Duchenne muscular dystrophy patients (Chan and Head, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Chan and Head, 2011.

claim: The generation of branched muscles in Drosophila identity mutants opens the possibility to investigate, in vivo, how physiological properties of branched fibres differ from morphologically normal fibres.
source: It opens the possibility to investigate, in vivo, how physiological properties of branched fibres differ from morphologically normal fibres and associated mechanical instability in an otherwise normal muscle pattern.
evidence: This is a statement about the potential application of the findings.
